newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo banks caution against alarming illiquidity.
newsitem.headline: Yugo banks caution against alarming illiquidity.

text.p: Yugoslavia's banks said on Tuesday they were alarmed by widespread illiquidity in the economy and urged monetary authorities to deal with accumulated inter-company debts which topped almost $7 billion in 1996.

Total short-term claims by Yugoslav companies, accumulated since 1994, reached 61.8 billion dinars at the end of 1996, said Novica Medenica, secretary of the Yugoslav Chamber of Commerce Banking Committee.

This compared with a total of 35.3 billion dinars in accumulated claims at the end of 1995. "Total liabilities stood at 101.34 billion dinars producing a 39.8 billion dinars ($6.94 billion) gap, which is the best indicator of illiquidity of our economy," Medenica said.
At the end of 1995, total accumulated liabilities stood at 55.2 billion dinars.
"This gap means that companies would have to sell out their entire inventories which stood at 37.4 billion dinars at the end of 1996 and still remain in the red," he said.

The National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) is preparing a project called multilateral compensation to settle at once most debts and claims. But economists cautioned the plan may be incomplete until the authorities find out how to tackle the first debtor who initiated the mess.

"They would either be forced to print all those missing dinars or transform the initial debt into a public debt, or issue some bonds, but the initiator needs to be punished," said an economist who asked not to be named.

"Multilateral compensation is difficult to perform when we lack some 40 billion dinars and there are no commodity inventories as collateral. Besides, we have an extreme financial non-discipline," said Zivota Mihajlovic, managing director of Vojvodjanska banka.
Bankers agreed multilateral compensation would be insufficient if carried out alone and it had to be accompanied by economic and legal measures.

Medenica insisted Yugoslavia's economy lacked financial stability although its constant capital accounted for 60 percent of total capital held by companies. "But cash accounts for only 3.2 percent of constant capital and 3.5 percent of their total working capital," he said.
Some bankers blamed the central bank for retaining a tough monetary stance over the last 2-1/2 years, but admitted tight policy finally produced price and the dinar stability in 1997.
Bankers praised the NBY for holding a tight grip over M1 money supply, but cautioned the grip was loosened in May when M1 shot up seven percent on April.
According to preliminary figures, M1 rose to 5.881 billion dinars in May from 5.561 billion in April.
The NBY was advised to retain its restrictive monetary stance and deal with financial non-discipline, but not to resort to the mint and print fresh dinars without backing.

Bankers suggested that companies and banks should cut their operations and increase efficiency in collecting claims. They also proposed that debts by farmers be rescheduled or even converted into public debt.

"The state must also look into possibilities to attract fresh capital for the economy, hurry up with the adoption of the privatisation law and settle outstanding issues to regulate Yugoslavia's status with international financial institutions," bankers said in their report.
